Source. The first witnessed `BDAT 0` increments `conn->state.data_chunks` from 0 to 1 and marks this command as `chunk_first`. That chunking state is later reused in two ways: it causes the first BDAT path to publish a shared DATA-input stream, and it makes a later bare `DATA` command hit the `Bad sequence of commands` path.

Because this is the first BDAT chunk and no chain exists yet, the server allocates a chain-backed `istream` object. ASan's allocation stack identifies this `i_stream_create_chain()` call as the origin of the later freed heap object.

The first BDAT command installs the chain stream from step 2 as global server DATA input and takes an owning reference. The call site at line 599 then unrefs `conn->state.data_chain_input`, leaving `conn->state.data_input` as the remaining live server-owned handle to this object.
Because this command is the first BDAT chunk, `cmd_data_next()` passes the shared chain stream in `conn->state.data_input` into the data-begin callback before continuing DATA processing.

The fuzz target stores the same stream pointer in file-static `state.data_input` without taking its own reference or clearing it when the server later destroys the connection's DATA input. This creates a raw second alias outside `conn->state.*`.

Later in the same witness, line 20 is bare `DATA`. `smtp_server_cmd_data()` allocates a new `data_cmd`, marks it as a one-shot `chunk_last` DATA command, and arms `cmd_data_destroy` before any input stream has been assigned to this new command.

When that later DATA command reaches its NEXT hook, the earlier BDAT sequence has left `conn->state.data_chunks > 0`, so the DATA command is rejected with `503 Bad sequence of commands` before `cmd_data_start_input()` can assign any main input of its own.

After the failed DATA command from step 7 finishes, its destroy hook takes this cleanup branch because `data_cmd->chunk_last` is true and the command did not reply successfully. In the vulnerable code the branch unconditionally destroys global `conn->state.data_input` / `data_chain_input`, even though this DATA command never acquired an input stream; the object freed is the earlier BDAT chain stream from steps 2-3. Commit `9f5e723974420af0014a397bb390b57f3b9a9431` fixes this by recording `data_cmd->main_input` and requiring `data_cmd->main_input == conn->state.data_input` before cleanup.

The fuzz callback's file-static alias was never cleared by step 8. When the earlier BDAT command is serviced again, `server_cmd_data_continue()` reloads `state.data_input` into local `data_input`, so the callback now holds a dangling pointer to the freed chain stream.

Sink. `server_cmd_data_continue()` immediately calls `i_stream_read(data_input)` on the dangling pointer from step 9, and `i_stream_read()` dereferences `stream->real_stream`. ASan records this exact line as the heap-use-after-free READ of size 8.

First project-side state derived from the witness SMTP command stream: the first `BDAT` command marks chunking as active on the connection and tags this command as the first chunk, which later enables both the shared DATA-input alias and the `DATA`-after-`BDAT` bad-sequence path.

Root cause. `cmd_data_destroy()` cleans global DATA-stream state based only on reply success / `chunk_last`; it never checks that the command being destroyed actually owns the current `conn->state.data_input`, so a later failed DATA command can free an earlier BDAT command's shared input stream.
Crash site. `server_cmd_data_continue()` re-enters `i_stream_read()` with a freed `struct istream *`, and `i_stream_read()` immediately dereferences `stream->real_stream`.
At the vulnerable cleanup site, the pointer passed to `i_stream_destroy(&conn->state.data_input)` is the same shared global DATA-input pointer later reloaded from fuzz-target state.
